title: Cold-to-Hot Transition Profiling and Loadgen Snapshotting Playbook
content:
Purpose:
This playbook documents a repeatable approach for profiling the cold->hot transition in the serving runtime and capturing deterministic loadgen "snapshots" so we can correlate first-token and early-tail behaviour with kernel selection, thermal state, and client-side variance. Goal is to make throughput claims reproducible across machines and model variants while surfacing subtle failure modes (PCIe stalls, kernel fallback thrash, quantized-path slow ramps).

Context / motivation:
- Many throughput regressions show up only during the first N minutes of a run (priming/cold KV cache behavior, allocator warmup, CUDA kernel JIT activity, memory compaction).
- Customers care about sustained tokens/sec but also about the cold-start tail on scale-ups and canary traffic.
- Existing harnesses capture steady-state but often miss the transition window.

High-level strategy:
1) Capture a deterministic snapshot of the client workload and RNG state.
2) Run a charge-of-requests warmup schedule that is parameterized (ramp, plateau, microbursts).
3) Simultaneously collect fine-grained server-side signals (GPU metrics, kernel selection logs, allocator traces, PCIe counters, nvtx spans) and client-side events (first-byte times, request timestamps, seed ids).
4) Repeat runs with controlled thermal boundary conditions (cold chassis, pre-heated, simulated fan curves) to detect thermal-triggered kernel switches.

Important signals to collect (minimum):
- Token throughput (tokens/sec) time series (1s resolution)
- Latency percentiles per token and per request (p50/p95/p99)
- First-token (TTFB) latency separately
- GPU SM util, memory utilization, encoder/decoder kernel time breakdowns
- PCIe transfer latencies and bandwidth counters (where available)
- CUDA kernel names and selected codepaths (JIT, cutlass, brgemm, fused-attn)
- Runtime logs for quantized execution path and fallback notices
- KV cache hit ratio and size over time
- System-level (dmesg) for OOM or driver warnings

Client loadgen snapshot format (recommended):
- Include the exact seed used for RNG and per-request seed offsets
- Include the sequence-length distribution and prompt prefix hashes
- Capture the initial request stream for the first 120s and store as a named snapshot.

Example loadgen snapshot (json blob used by our harness):
{
  "snapshot_id": "snapshot-2025-02-11-01",
  "seed": "784321",
  "requests": [
    {"prompt_hash": "a1b2c3", "seq_len": 32, "role": "inference"},
    {"prompt_hash": "d4e5f6", "seq_len": 128, "role": "batch-cold"}
  ],
  "client_version": "loadgen-v2.3"
}

Warmup schedule template:
- Phase 0 (clock sync): 30s of low-frequency probes to align clocks and establish baseline latencies.
- Phase 1 (microburst priming): 45s of repeated 8-concurrency microbursts at 2x target qps to populate KV cache + kernel caches.
- Phase 2 (ramp): linear ramp from 10% -> 100% over 90s.
- Phase 3 (plateau): sustain target load for at least 10 minutes to claim steady-state numbers.
- Phase 4 (cooldown snapshot): stop sending new requests and capture ring buffers + nvprof sample.

Runbook (step-by-step):
1) Prepare machine: reboot into known kernel, clear persistent DKMS caches if testing JIT variations, reset GPU power cap to standard value. Note: always record BIOS/fan profile.
2) Upload loadgen snapshot to the client host. Record OS load, dmesg head, and driver versions.
3) Start system resource collectors: node-exporter, nvidia-smi loop, perf record for top kernels, and nvtx tracing.
4) Start server-side trace capture (open telemetry span + local NVTX markers around model load and first request).
5) Run clock sync probe (phase 0) and validate timestamps within 5ms. If not, re-evaluate NTP/PTP.
6) Launch warmup schedule. Observe first-token latencies carefully in the first 30s.
7) After plateau, take full snapshot: GPU state, allocator histograms, JVM/pyprof stacks (if applicable), and copy loadgen trace.
8) Tear down reproducibly, change only one variable (e.g., quant flavor, power cap, batcher config) and repeat.

Analysis guidance:
- Use the snapshot id as the primary key for joining client and server traces.
- Correlate abrupt throughput jumps/dips with kernel change logs (grep for "kernel switched" and timestamp).
- If p99 at minute 0 >> p99 at minute 5, suspect JIT or cache miss patterns in first 30s.
- Look for PCIe transfer size spikes coincident with spikes in service time: may indicate host->device page faults or unexpected host-side staging.

Common failure modes and mitigations:
- Flaky repeatability due to nondeterministic client RNG: enforce snapshot seed and per-request IDs.
- Thermal-induced kernel fallback: reproduce with artificial fan curve and capture power/SM clocks.
- Memory allocator fragmentation: capture allocator histograms and prefer warmup that exercises large allocations early.
- Batcher head-of-line blocking: randomize request sequence lengths in early priming to avoid pathological batching queues.

Experiment matrix (example):
- Variables: quant-mode (fp16/int8), power-cap (200W/250W/default), warmup-length (2m/10m), batcher-policy (fixed/adaptive), client-concurrency (1/8/32).
- Keep other variables fixed and run each cell 3x with new snapshot id.

Repro checklist (short):
- [ ] snapshot_id embedded in every produced artifact (logs, traces, metrics)
- [ ] seeds recorded and preserved
- [ ] machine precondition recorded (driver/BIOS/fan profile)
- [ ] NVTX spans present around model load & first-request windows
- [ ] Clock sync verified before run

Example quick troubleshooting snippets:
- Identify kernel ramp: grep -n "kernel:" server_trace.log | sed -n '1,200p'
- Join client & server traces by snapshot id: jq -r '.snapshot_id' loadgen_trace.json
- Check PCIe stalls: sudo perf record -e pcie/pcie_port_stall/ -a sleep 120 (where supported)

Open questions / TO-DOs:
- Evaluate if loader prefetch (prefetching large KV blocks) helps amortize early PCIe latency.
- Add automated thermal stress mode in CI to detect kernel fallbacks across model catalog nightly.
- Determine the minimum plateau duration for stable p99 claims per model family.

Notes to reviewers:
- This doc is intentionally pragmatic and slightly opinionated (we bias to longer, slightly over-provisioned warmups to get deterministic baselines). If you prefer leaner customer-facing numbers we can add a reduced warmup variant.
- See linked artifacts for the tracking ticket and prototype PR that adds snapshot id propagation to existing traces.

-- Maya
